item.title: Boselawa signs with the Fijian Drua
item.description: The Swire Shipping Fijian Drua have signed Nadroga centre Kavekini Boselawa as a Senior Development Player after his impressive performances in this year’s Skipper Cup. Boselawa caught the attention of new Drua head coach Brad Mooar and club officials during Nadroga’s Round 1 match in Lautoka, earning an opportunity to take the next step in his rugby career.
item.content:encoded:
The Swire Shipping Fijian Drua have signed Nadroga centre Kavekini Boselawa as a Senior Development Player after his impressive performances in this year’s Skipper Cup.

Boselawa caught the attention of new Drua head coach Brad Mooar and club officials during Nadroga’s Round 1 match in Lautoka, earning an opportunity to take the next step in his rugby career.

The signing highlights the Drua’s commitment to creating pathways for talented local players to progress into Shop N Save Super Rugby Pacific.

Boselawa, who hails from Naduri in Macuata and has maternal ties to Nadrala in Nadroga, is a relative newcomer to rugby. He played soccer throughout his school years before taking up rugby at the age of 19 while studying Land Surveying at Fiji National University.

He quickly established himself with Nadrala Rugby Club and Nadroga, developing a reputation as a strong and versatile back. Boselawa said he was grateful for the opportunity and credited his father for influencing his rugby journey.

“My Tou has had the biggest influence on me, as a man and on my rugby journey,” he said.

Mooar said Boselawa immediately stood out when he watched him play in Lautoka and praised his physical ability and adaptability.

The 2026 Skipper Cup campaign now provides Boselawa with another chance to impress, with Nadroga facing Navosa at Lawaqa Park this Friday.

He will hope to use the opportunity to move closer to earning a place in the Drua’s main squad.

item.title: Kadavu to move games
item.description: KADAVU Rugby Union (KRU) has been forced to abandon home advantage for the remainder of its Skipper Cup campaign after worsening weather made travel to the island increasingly unsafe. The KRU confirmed yesterday that its remaining three home matches will be relocated to Viti Levu because of continued wet weather, rough seas and strong winds affecting maritime travel to and within Kadavu.
item.content:encoded:
KADAVU Rugby Union (KRU) has been forced to abandon home advantage for the remainder of its Skipper Cup campaign after worsening weather made travel to the island increasingly unsafe.

The KRU confirmed yesterday that its remaining three home matches will be relocated to Viti Levu because of continued wet weather, rough seas and strong winds affecting maritime travel to and within Kadavu.

The decision comes after KRU made history by bringing Skipper Cup and Subrails Marama Championship matches to Kadavu, allowing the teams to play in front of their home supporters.

KRU president Lynda Tabuya said the decision was not taken lightly.

“We were immensely proud to make history by bringing the Skipper Cup and Subrails Marama Championship matches home to Kadavu, and nothing compares to playing before our own people on our own home soil,” Tabuya said.

“However, the welfare and safety of our players, visiting teams, supporters and the travelling public must come first.”

The Fiji Meteorological Service’s continuing weather warnings have added to concerns over the safety and reliability of maritime travel.

The difficult conditions have also affected supporters travelling from Viti Levu to Kadavu, as well as residents moving by sea from different parts of the island to attend matches.

KRU said relocating the fixtures would provide greater certainty for teams and supporters while allowing the union to tap into its strong supporter base on Viti Levu.

The school holidays could also provide an opportunity for families to attend the matches.

Kadavu’s first relocated home fixture will be against Lautoka at Churchill Park in Lautoka this Saturday.

KRU is calling on its supporters across the Western Division and Viti Levu to turn out in numbers and back the Kadavu side.

Venues for the other two relocated home fixtures will be announced once confirmed.

item.content:encoded:
THIRTY of Fiji’s best emerging schoolgirl rugby players are set to receive scholarships under a landmark new pathway program that began yesterday in Nadi and will continue until Friday — marking a breakthrough moment for the development of women’s rugby in the country.

For years, one of the biggest challenges in the women’s game has been identifying talented young players and ensuring they do not disappear from the system before reaching the national stage.

Now, Fiji Rugby has taken a major step towards changing that.

Through the Na Soko competition and its talent identification and development pathway program, the best players from the North, South, East and West are being brought together, assessed and developed under one structured system.

By the end of the week, 30 of the best performers will be selected for scholarships and another 30 identified for further development.

Fiji Rugby Women’s academy coach Tavaita Rowati said the program represented an important step in finally establishing a clearer pathway from school’s rugby to the highest level.

The players are first identified through the Raluve competition in the under-16 and U18 grades before progressing to the second phase through Na Soko.

There, they undergo screening by Fiji Rugby’s strength and conditioning department and receive further coaching and development through the academy programmed.

“Today marks the beginning of selection as we go through the process of selecting 30 schoolgirls for scholarship and 30 for development,” Rowati said.

The program, supported by the Ministry of Education and Fiji Rugby, is designed to ensure Fiji’s best young female players are no longer left to develop without direction.

Rowati said the selected players would be monitored through the national high-performance and academy systems.

The goal is to build a steady pipeline of players capable of progressing into the Fiji women’s national sevens and 15s programs.

For women’s rugby in Fiji, the significance goes beyond the 30 scholarships.

It represents the achievement of a long-needed goal — the creation of a genuine, structured pathway for talented schoolgirls to move from schools’ rugby towards the national jersey.

With the country’s best young players now being identified, supported and monitored, the Na Soko competition could mark the beginning of an exciting new era for Fiji women’s rugby.

item.title: Time for Fiji to build for sport’s future
item.description: THE events across Fiji’s sporting fields over the past week should not be dismissed as simply another disruption caused by bad weather. From the muddy HFC Bank National Stadium to the cancellation of a national secondary schools netball championship, and from thousands of supporters being turned away from a sold-out stadium to a northern school making history without a proper ground or gym, one me
item.content:encoded:
THE events across Fiji’s sporting fields over the past week should not be dismissed as simply another disruption caused by bad weather.

From the muddy HFC Bank National Stadium to the cancellation of a national secondary schools netball championship, and from thousands of supporters being turned away from a sold-out stadium to a northern school making history without a proper ground or gym, one message is clear.

Fiji needs bigger and better sporting facilities.

The Vodafone Super Deans and Raluve Championship finals over the weekend provided the most visible example.

Days of continuous rain left the HFC Bank National Stadium playing surface soggy and muddy. The under-18 third-place playoff was shifted to Burchurst Park in an effort to protect the ground before the U18 final.

Yet by the second match, the surface had deteriorated badly.

It was unfortunate to watch young players contest national honours in such conditions. A national final should be the pinnacle of a student’s sporting career, played on a surface worthy of the occasion.

The rain is not the real problem. Rain is part of life in Fiji.

The question is whether our sporting infrastructure is capable of coping with it.

For several years, the Deans and Raluve finals have attracted more supporters than the national stadium can accommodate. Thousands turn up, only to be turned away at the gates once the venue is full.

Every year, parents and family members are left outside, unable to watch their sons and daughters compete for national honours.

A sold-out stadium should be a success story. It demonstrates the extraordinary passion Fijians have for school sport.

But repeatedly turning away thousands of supporters is also evidence that demand has outgrown our facilities.

Earlier last week, the effects of the weather were being felt elsewhere.

The Vodafone Central 1 Kaji and Kajiana Championship at Saint Marcellin School in Vatuwaqa underwent hourly evaluations because of continuous rain and deteriorating ground conditions.

Organisers carefully monitored the surface for the safety and well-being of the students. Fortunately, the tournament was completed without serious injuries or mishaps.

The Crest Fiji Secondary Schools Netball Championships was not as fortunate.

The competition was forced to end after the quarter-finals last Friday when the Jai Narayan College grounds became unplayable following days of rain.

Fiji Secondary Schools Netball Association president Navitalai Naivalu said the decision was made for the safety and well-being of the students and called for serious consideration to be given to building suitable netball facilities.

The turnout at national championships and rallies around the country shows the depth of interest in the sport. Netball is Fiji’s most popular women’s sport, yet its facilities have not kept pace with participation.

Fiji Pearls head coach Michelle Parsons made an equally important point.

She said organisers had done their best, but the players who had worked their way through to the national championship deserved a facility that allowed them to focus on their game and skills.

They should not have to worry about slipping, losing their footing or falling awkwardly when landing from a jump.

That is what a national facility should provide: an environment where athletes can concentrate on performing, rather than protecting themselves from the playing surface.

The lack of facilities is not confined to Suva.

Navatu Secondary School’s historic run to the Vodafone Super Deans U19 final should be celebrated as one of the year’s greatest sporting stories.

The school became the first northern team to reach the national U19 final — despite not having a proper school ground or gym for its players to train.

If a school facing those challenges can reach a national final, imagine what could be achieved with proper facilities.

The success of Navatu Secondary School also highlights a wider issue. Northern schools often struggle to remain consistently competitive against better-resourced schools in the Central and Western divisions.

Talent has never been the problem but rather access to proper facilities.

item.title: Tailevu hails historic treble against Nadi
item.description: HISTORY was made in the Fiji Rugby Union provincial competition as Fresh Choice Tailevu and McDonald’s Nadi produced a remarkable clean sweep of draws, with all three matches ending level at full time during round four of the Subrails Marama Cup Championship and Skipper Cup competition at Churchill Park in Lautoka. Tailevu Rugby Union’s president Joe Rodan Snr believes last Friday’s three-way draw
item.content:encoded:
HISTORY was made in the Fiji Rugby Union provincial competition as Fresh Choice Tailevu and McDonald’s Nadi produced a remarkable clean sweep of draws, with all three matches ending level at full time during round four of the Subrails Marama Cup Championship and Skipper Cup competition at Churchill Park in Lautoka.

Tailevu Rugby Union’s president Joe Rodan Snr believes last Friday’s three-way draw against McDonald’s Nadi was a historic moment for Fiji’s provincial rugby.

The Tailevu and Nadi under-20 sides played to an 18-all draw, while the women’s match ended 24-all before the senior men produced another thriller, finishing 19-all.

Rodan said he could not recall such an occurrence in the history of Fiji’s provincial rugby competitions.

“It is history in the making where we have three games and three draws,” Rodan said.

“I don’t think this has ever happened in the history of Fiji Rugby Provincial competition.

“Three games and three draws in the under-20, Marama Cup and Skipper Cup, and that shows the knowledge and strength that our players have displayed out there.”

Rodan believes the quality of rugby showcased by both Tailevu and Nadi should encourage more local supporters to attend provincial matches.

He said the standard of the Skipper Cup and Marama Cup competitions had improved significantly, with local players proving they could deliver entertaining and competitive rugby.

“Like I said, we pay a lot of money to go watch the Flying Fijians play overseas, but what Tailevu and Nadi showed last Friday in the Marama and Skipper Cup competition is a really high standard,” he said.

“I wish that our local supporters and spectators will support the Skipper Cup competition because the Skipper Cup has improved a lot.”

Rodan said he would like to see greater support for provincial rugby and more spectators turning up to watch local players in action.

“To me, I like to see more local players and local spectators’ step in to support Skipper Cup because we have got a high standard of rugby nowadays,” he said.

Despite the draw against Nadi, Rodan was already looking ahead to Tailevu’s next challenge with Rodan confident his side can secure victory.

“We will take on Naitasiri and we will beat Naitasiri at Ratu Cakobau Park this week,” he said.

item.title: Sleepless nights fuel Dennis’ Deans dream
item.description: SLEEPLESS nights and the challenges of boarding school life could not stop Ratu Kadavulevu School under-15 player Dennis Murray from helping his team achieve Vodafone Super Deans Championship glory. The young Murray was part of the RKS side that edged Marist Brothers High School 17-15 in the U15 final, producing a performance that brought him one step closer to his dream of following his elder bro
item.content:encoded:
SLEEPLESS nights and the challenges of boarding school life could not stop Ratu Kadavulevu School under-15 player Dennis Murray from helping his team achieve Vodafone Super Deans Championship glory.

The young Murray was part of the RKS side that edged Marist Brothers High School 17-15 in the U15 final, producing a performance that brought him one step closer to his dream of following his elder brother, Fijian Drua flanker Motikai Murray.

For Dennis, the title was more than just another schoolboy rugby achievement. It was a reminder that the sacrifices he is making at school could eventually help him reach the same heights as his brother, who has played Super Rugby Pacific for the Drua and represented the Flying Fijians.

Dennis admits boarding school life has not always been easy.

“Some challenges I face in school are sleepless nights and sometimes not being fed well, but that’s boarding school life and it takes being patient,” he said.

Those challenges, however, have only strengthened his determination.

He says Motikai remains a major influence on his development and continues to encourage him to work hard.

“He always encourages me to play hard so I can reach his level. My dream is to one day play with him.”

The Deans triumph was therefore a significant milestone for the young player, who also thanked God for the victory and the talent given to his elder brother.

“I thank God for today’s win and for also giving my elder brother the talent he has.”

While Dennis celebrated his first taste of Deans success, Motikai has been making his own statement on the rugby field in New Zealand.

The Drua flanker has been in blistering form in the National Provincial Championship, performances that have earned him a recall to the Flying Fijians squad for the defence of the Pacific Nations Cup.

For Dennis, his brother’s success provides a powerful example of what can be achieved.

The sleepless nights may continue, but so too will the dream of one day playing alongside Motikai at the highest level.

item.title: Bowl to honour ex-Bati rep
item.description: FOR a player whose career ended far sooner than he would have wanted, Tui Kamikamica will have a lasting place in Fiji rugby league history. The former Melbourne Storm forward and Fiji Bati captain will be honoured on Saturday when the Kaiviti Silktails and Melbourne Storm contest the inaugural Tui Kamikamica Bowl at Churchill Park in Lautoka.
item.content:encoded:
FOR a player whose career ended far sooner than he would have wanted, Tui Kamikamica will have a lasting place in Fiji rugby league history.

The former Melbourne Storm forward and Fiji Bati captain will be honoured on Saturday when the Kaiviti Silktails and Melbourne Storm contest the inaugural Tui Kamikamica Bowl at Churchill Park in Lautoka.

The perpetual Bowl comes just days after Kamikamica announced his immediate retirement on medical grounds, abruptly ending a remarkable career that produced 142 NRL appearances for Storm and 23 Tests for Fiji.

His journey from Fiji to the top of the Australian game included two NRL premierships, 15 finals appearances, grand-final appearances in 2024 and 2025, and Storm Life Membership this year.

He also captained the Fiji Bati from 2023.

Kamikamica said having the fixture named after him was a special honour for his family.

“It is an honour for me and my family to be named for the Bowl games between the Silktails and Storm this week and for all future games,” he said.

“I truly appreciate all the love and support and I am looking forward to coming over for the game.”

For Silktails founder and chairman Petero Civoniceva, Kamikamica’s career represents exactly why the club was established — to show young Fijians that a pathway from the village and school grounds to the NRL is possible.

“For a young player in Fiji to be able to see the journey Tui has taken, from Fiji to the NRL, winning Premierships and ultimately captaining his country, shows them what is possible,” Civoniceva said.

Kamikamica’s playing career may have ended abruptly, but his legacy will continue through a fixture carrying his name.

The inaugural Bowl, part of the NSW Jersey Flegg Cup, kicks off at 11am at Churchill Park on Saturday.

For one of Fiji’s most distinguished modern rugby league players, it marks the beginning of a new chapter in a game he has served with distinction.

item.title: Navatu coach challenges North: Prepare to win
item.description: NAVATU Secondary School under-19 head coach Alipate Ravulo has thrown down the challenge to schools and teams in the North — prepare to win, not simply to participate. Ravulo’s message comes after his side created history as the first northern school team to ever reach the Vodafone Super Deans Championship U19 final, becoming the lone northern school to carry the division’s hopes on the biggest st
item.content:encoded:
NAVATU Secondary School under-19 head coach Alipate Ravulo has thrown down the challenge to schools and teams in the North — prepare to win, not simply to participate.

Ravulo’s message comes after his side created history as the first northern school team to ever reach the Vodafone Super Deans Championship U19 final, becoming the lone northern school to carry the division’s hopes on the biggest stage of Fiji’s secondary school rugby competition.

For Ravulo, the achievement is proof that northern schools have the ability to compete with their Viti Levu counterparts when given the right preparation.

His challenge to other northern teams is simple but profound: preparation must be purposeful.

“Prepare to win, don’t prepare to participate,” Ravulo said.

He believes preparation must go beyond physical conditioning and rugby skills, with teams needing to cater for the physical, mental and spiritual aspects of their players.

Ravulo said northern teams should not see themselves as inferior to schools from Viti Levu.

“We are all the same. Whether we are from Viti Levu or Vanua Levu, we are all human. We just need to prepare well,” he said.

More importantly, Ravulo believes northern schools should have no excuses after Navatu’s historic run.

The school does not have its own rugby ground or gym and has had to work with very limited resources, yet its U19 side has fought its way into the national final.

If Navatu can reach the biggest stage despite those limitations, Ravulo believes schools in the North with better facilities and greater resources should be capable of achieving even more.

“Navatu’s achievement should tell every school in the North that it is possible,” is the message behind Ravulo’s challenge.

His words carry added weight because Navatu’s campaign has demonstrated what can be achieved when belief, discipline and preparation are placed ahead of circumstances.

The message was echoed by his captain and standout player, Vilimone Kanawabu, who has emerged as one of the competition’s leading performers.

Despite attending school in the North, Kanawabu broke into the Fiji Schoolboys team last year, showing that talent from Vanua Levu can earn recognition at national level.

Kanawabu believes the formula for achieving rugby goals is equally straightforward.

He said unwavering faith, coupled with hard work, was the secret behind reaching one’s goals.
